column13: And as it is said (Amos 3:2): "You only have I known... therefore I will visit upon you...", which the Gemara concludes is executed in mercy, as written in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (4a), for yada'ti ("I have known") shares the root of moda ("kinsman/beloved") [Ruth 3:2], meaning love, therefore efkod ("I will visit") means with active visitation and providence, not by withdrawing providence and abandoning them to the blind course of nature (ha-teva = 86), which equals the numerical value of Elohim (86) through which the nations of the world are judged.

column11: Sotah 12b: ‘The Gemara answers: This teaches that prior to this, they took Moses around to all the Egyptian wet nurses and he did not agree to nurse from any of them, as he said: Shall a mouth that in the future will speak with the Divine Presence actually nurse something impure? And this is as it is written: “Whom shall one teach knowledge? And whom shall one make understand the message?” (Isaiah 28:9). column11: Nedarim 22b: ‘Rav Adda, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said: Had Israel not sinned in earlier times they would have been given the five books of the Torah and the book of Joshua alone. column13: For the Written Torah is “the shining-forth of Hashem’s light to Israel at the Giving of the Torah,” by which they became “free of the evil inclination”; and then the Written Torah alone would have sufficed, as they said [in Nedarim 22b] that “had they not sinned, there would have been given to them only the [Five Books of the] Torah and the Book of Yehoshua” — [the latter being] “the apportionment of the Land of Israel.” — for it [Yehoshua] is the apportionment of Eretz Yisrael.”

column15: Why does the section of vows begin “And Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes” (Numbers 30:2) rather than “And the Lord spoke”? Because while all other mitzvot apply fixed boundaries equally at all times, vows (nedarim) depend upon each person’s inner discernment (binah) of where his own heart requires an individual protective fence to guard its holiness.

column11: Zohar, Miketz 12:194-206: ‘The brothers were afraid on account of their sin in having stolen Joseph, for had they not sinned they would not have had any cause to fear; for it is only a man’s sins that break his courage and deprive him of strength, the reason being that the good prompter is at the same time unnerved, and left powerless to contend with the evil prompter. column11: Sukkah 52b: ‘The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: If this scoundrel, the evil inclination, accosted you, seeking to tempt you to sin, drag it to the study hall and study Torah. If it is like a stone, it will be dissolved by the Torah. If it is like iron, it will be shattered. The Gemara elaborates: If it is like stone, it will be dissolved, as it is written: “Ho, everyone who is thirsty, come you for the water” (Isaiah 55:1), water in this context meaning Torah; and it is written: “Stones were worn by water” (Job 14:19). If it is like iron, it will be shattered, as it is written: “Is not My word like fire, says the Lord; and like a hammer that shatters rock” (Jeremiah 23:29).’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 3, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sukkah 52b) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written (Sukkah 52b): " ‘If this vile one confronts you, drag him to the study hall’, and that is the place where novel halakhot are innovated. And the Book of Deuteronomy (Mishneh Torah)”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For in words of Torah there is also the perception of the Secret which is Hashem, meaning the ultimate truth of Hashem, blessed be He, and cleaving to Him is that very delight which is a foretaste of the World to Come. column15: "And Hashem said to Avram: Go for yourself, etc., to the land that I will show you," (Genesis 12:1), "For I will pour water upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land; I will pour My spirit upon your seed, and My blessing upon your offspring" (Isaiah 44:3). This verse speaks concerning our father Avraham, peace be upon him, whose soul thirsted continually, watching, hoping, and yearning to know Who is He Who created all this; and he wondered over the early generations who perished and were blotted out from the world without hope.

column11: Megillah 31b: ‘Abaye said: They taught this only with regard to the curses that are recorded in Leviticus, but with regard to the curses that are recorded in Deuteronomy, one may interrupt them by having two different people read them. column11: Arakhin 16b: ‘§ The Gemara asks: Until where is the minimum limit of suffering? What is the least amount pain that is included in the definition of suffering? Rava the Younger objects to this, and some say Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani objects: The Sages said an even greater statement than this, i.e., that even lesser inconvenience is still considered suffering: Even if people intended that they would dilute his wine with hot water, but they accidentally diluted it for him with cold water, it is considered suffering. column11: Zohar, Bereshit 32:330-35:339: ‘the light being called day and the darkness night, as it says, “And God called the light day and the darkness he called night.” This is the darkness that is attached to night, which has no light of its own, although it comes from the side of the primordial fire which is also called “darkness”. It remains dark until it is illumined from the side of day. Day illumines night, and night will not be light of itself until the time of which it is written, “the night shineth as the day, the darkness is even as the light” (Ps. 139, 12).’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 3, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Bereshit 32:330-35:339) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written in the holy Zohar (Part I, 31a end). column11: Kiddushin 39b: ‘As it is taught in a baraita that Rabbi Ya’akov says: There is not a single mitzva written in the Torah whose reward is stated alongside it, which is not dependent on the resurrection of the dead, i.e., the reward is actually bestowed in the World-to-Come, after the resurrection of the dead. column11: Kiddushin 40a: ‘And with regard to bringing peace it is written: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Psalms 34:15). column11: Berakhot 54a: ‘The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). For prayer is termed fear/awe, as written in Berakhot 9b on the verse "They shall fear You while the sun endures" (Psalms 72:5); and words of Torah are joy, as written: "The statutes of Hashem are right, rejoicing the heart" (Psalms 19:9); and these two unite, as written in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (chapter 3): "I feared out of my joy, etc.,"

And "hearkens to the voice of His servant"—this is the prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur), who stands like a servant before the King (Section 210).

column11: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 1. English translation of source: “‘Our teachers taught: For three transgressions women die at the time of childbirth. All three have their basis in the Torah: niddah, as it is written, ‘If a woman has a flow [of blood]’; challah, ‘The first of your dough’; and the lighting of a lamp, as it is written, ‘You shall call Shabbos a delight’—this refers to kindling the Shabbos lamp. If you should say that one might sit in darkness, that is not delight, for those who descend to Gehinnom are judged in darkness, as it says, ‘A land of deepest gloom, like darkness.’’ The Midrash continues: ‘Why were women commanded concerning these three mitzvos? ... She caused [Adam] to die and shed his blood ... She defiled the challah of the world ... She extinguished Adam’s lamp, as it is written, ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord’; therefore she must attend to kindling the lamp.’” Context and connection: The source develops both sides of Rav Tzadok’s argument: the three practices address the loss introduced by the first sin, while light is the positive image of Shabbos restoration. The relevant lamp passage occurs in Noach 1 in the commonly indexed Sefaria edition; Rav Tzadok's printed numbering differs.
column13: “Time is composed of day and night, and so too is human life: light and darkness, ascending and descending, as is known from the Baal Shem Tov's teaching on the verse: "Seven times does the righteous fall and rise up" (Proverbs 24:16). For seven days constitute one week, and thereafter those same seven days recur in cycle. Indeed, even during the period of darkness one needs the light of the moon or the stars, which is also recognized as light (Pesachim 2a), so that it not be total obscurity. And inside one's house, one requires the light of a candle”
column14: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 38:1
column15: “Now therefore, I pray You, if I have found grace in Your sight, show me now Your ways, that I may know You” (Exodus 33:13). To Moses the Blessed Name revealed the deepest clarity beneath all garments of concealment—teaching that even when an event appears outwardly as stern judgment or hiddenness, within its innermost core resides the glory of Heaven and boundless compassion for Israel.

column11: Job 10:21–22. English translation of source: “‘Before I depart—and do not return—to the land of darkness and the shadow of death: a land of thick gloom, like utter darkness; of deathly shadow and disorder, where even its radiance is like darkness.’” Context and connection: The surrounding verse describes the realm of death, not the laws of Shabbos. Tanchuma borrows this vivid image for Gehinnom. Rav Tzadok then treats the light of a Shabbos lamp as more than physical convenience: it represents an opposite spiritual condition, one of order, comfort and revealed divine presence.
column13: “The Holy One, blessed be He, His glory fills the whole earth, and there is no place devoid of Him, only that He is in deep concealment, "He made darkness His secret place" (Psalms 18:12). And when this recognition shines into man's heart—how Hashem fills the whole earth with His glory— this is termed "He brought us forth from darkness to a great light," as recited in the Haggadah.”

column15: And as taught in the Gemara (Niddah 30b): A fetus in its mother's womb has a candle burning above its head, gazing from one end of the world to the other, with nothing concealed from it, and all words of Torah are revealed before it.

column11: Genesis 1:2; Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2. English translation of source: “Genesis 1:2: ‘The earth was unformed and empty, darkness was over the face of the deep, and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.’ Midrash Tanchuma, Bo 2: ‘Rabbi Nechemiah said: [The darkness of Egypt came] from the darkness of Gehinnom, for it is said, ‘A land of thick gloom, like darkness, of deathly shadow and no order.’ ... With what are the wicked covered in Gehinnom? With darkness. Just as an earthenware jar is covered with an earthenware lid, so these wicked ones, whose deeds are in the dark, are covered by the Holy One, blessed be He, with the deep, which is darkness, as it says: ‘And darkness was upon the face of the deep.’ This is Gehinnom.’” Context and connection: In the verse, darkness precedes creation’s illumination. In the Midrash it becomes a moral image: a person concealed in wrongdoing encounters concealment. Rav Tzadok juxtaposes this with the contrary possibility that divine judgment may awaken recognition and thereby itself be experienced as light.

column13: “By day one gives precedence to light: "He forms light and creates darkness"; while at night one reverses it: "He rolls away light before darkness and darkness before light": for each blessing emphasizes the dominant quality of its own hour; and relative to the night, cessation and darkness take precedence over the light of day, matching the physical Creation of the cosmos: first came darkness and then came light (Shabbat 77b); for one who stands in darkness encounters darkness first, followed by the light.”
column14: Tiferet Yosef, Noach 1:8

And so it is taught in the Holy Zohar (Bereishit 26a): “And a mist rose up from the earth” — this refers to the letters Aleph-Dalet of the divine Name Adonai. And all of this reflects the yearning cry that creation possessed from the very initial awakening of divine Will, wherein Hashem willed the actualization of the worlds.

column11: Pesachim 54a. English translation of source: “‘This is no difficulty: one statement concerns our fire and one concerns the fire of Gehinnom. Our fire [was created] at the close of Shabbos; the fire of Gehinnom, on the eve of Shabbos. But was the fire of Gehinnom created on the eve of Shabbos? Was it not taught that seven things were created before the world: the Torah, repentance, the Garden of Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Sanctuary, and the name of the Messiah? ... Rabbi Yose says: The fire created by the Holy One, blessed be He, on the second day never goes out, as it says, ‘Their fire shall not be quenched.’ ... Why was ‘for it was good’ not said on the second day? Because the fire of Gehinnom was created then.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok deliberately focuses on the expression ‘the light of Gehinnom.’ He is not denying its punitive aspect. He argues that for one who accepts the truth of the judgment, the confrontation can illuminate what was previously hidden. The paradox depends on distinguishing revelatory light from the comfort of an ordinary flame.
column13: “Our Sages of blessed memory also taught (Nedarim 8b) that in the future there will be no Gehinnom; rather, the sun will be removed from its sheath—the righteous, etc., and the wicked, etc. This follows the principle: 'The righteous shall walk in them, while sinners shall stumble in them.' Likewise, they taught (Shabbat 88b) that for those who turn to the left in Torah it becomes a potion of death; 'evil pursues sinners,' for the sin itself becomes the punishment.”

column11: Eruvin 19a; Isaiah 66:24. English translation of source: “‘But did Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish not say: The wicked do not return in repentance even at the entrance to Gehinnom, as it is said, ‘They shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men who rebel against Me’ [Isaiah 66:24]? It does not say ‘who rebelled’ but ‘who rebel’—they go on rebelling forever! There is no difficulty: this statement concerns the sinners of Israel, and that statement the sinners of the nations of the world.’” Context and connection: The distinction concerns how suffering is received, not merely whether punishment is severe. Rav Tzadok uses the sugya to explain that for a person who refuses teshuvah, judgment remains darkness because it produces no renewed recognition of Hashem.
column13: “Transgressions within the soul of an Israelite are not an essential acquisition, but merely incidental, and therefore they are subject to redemption, as it is stated: 'And He shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities' (Psalms 130:8).”

column15: For on the Sabbath day the Blessed Name engages with the supernal realms, as taught in the Holy Zohar (Yitro 88b); therefore, do not distract your mind with lowly matters such as bodily needs, but merely gaze at whatever the Blessed Name bestows.

column11: Eruvin 19a; Psalms 84:7. English translation of source: “‘What, then, of the verse, ‘Those who pass through the valley of weeping make it a spring’ [Psalm 84:7]? That refers to those who are then liable to punishment in Gehinnom; but our father Avraham comes, raises them up, and receives them. He does not leave the circumcised among Israel [there], except for one who entered a forbidden union with a gentile woman; his foreskin is drawn over, and Avraham does not recognize him.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok draws attention to the limited character of punishment in this account, contrasting it with perpetual obstinacy. The sugya provides the language of Avraham’s rescue; the further interpretation that acknowledgment of judgment itself becomes light is Rav Tzadok’s explanation.
column13: “Whoever is a Torah scholar gathers souls and collects holy sparks from sacred souls that have been scattered into the depths of the great abyss. Through his Torah study, every spoken word of Torah extracts those souls affiliated with him, as it is written: "and he that wins souls is wise" (Proverbs 11:30). And he also extracts his own soul, as written (Midrash Rabbah, introduction to Eichah): "the illumination within it returns him to good."”
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 15:4

column11: Song of Songs 8:13; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 8:13. English translation of source: “Song of Songs 8:13: ‘You who dwell in the gardens, the companions listen for your voice; let me hear it.’ Shir HaShirim Rabbah, on this verse: ‘Rabbi Yirmeyah said in the name of Rabbi Chiyya the Great: Two companions who engage with one another in a matter of halachah and yield to one another in the argument—of them Scripture says, ‘Then those who fear the Lord spoke with one another, and the Lord paid attention and heard’ [Malachi 3:16]. ... Rabbi Yudan said: When Israel read Torah together in groups, ‘Let me hear your voice’; otherwise, ‘Flee, my beloved.’ Rabbi Zeira said: When Israel recite Shema with one mouth, one voice, and one melody, ‘Let me hear your voice’; otherwise, ‘Flee, my beloved.’’” Context and connection: The Midrash expounds the verse as God listening to shared Torah study and to the united recital of Shema. Rav Tzadok takes this image into the special atmosphere of Shabbos, and interprets the gardens as a hint to Gan Eden and its levels of sanctity.
column13: ““A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day: It is good to give thanks to Hashem” (Psalms 92:1-2). My revered grandfather, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, explained regarding this that the ultimate purpose of the creation of heaven and earth is the Sabbath day. Meaning, during the six workdays, man acts and toils, and it appears to him that he himself is piercing the concealment and recognizing the revelation of the Kingdom of Heaven in the world. And afterwards, on the Sabbath day, man realizes: “What was the world lacking? Rest; the Sabbath came, rest came” (Rashi on Genesis 2:2) — meaning, he recognizes that even the very strength to toil was entirely granted by Hashem, and he recognizes that in truth, from the perspective of Hashem, all is without limit and without boundary; and that these boundaries which Hashem instituted were solely because He desired to bestow good upon His creations, wishing that the Jew should coronate Hashem through free choice, actively choosing the good and despising the bad. For had the revelation of the Kingdom of Heaven been completely explicit, there would be no free will whatsoever, as all would clearly recognize that it is impossible to flee from the Source of Life; therefore Hashem established these limitations.”

column15: To the hearts of Israel, it proceeds level by level, first by way of the leaders of Israel, just as the Torah was given to Moshe and afterwards he taught it to the leaders of Israel until it finally reached the common folk, just in the same way each soul in Israel first receives in his consciousness [da’at-Moshe] until the Kedusha is fixed in all his limbs and organs, as it is written [Malachi, 3:16], “then they that feared God spoke with one another, God heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before Him,” meaning that it was carved into the hearts of the children of Israel.

column11: Shabbat 32a; Proverbs 20:27. English translation of source: “‘I called you ‘first,’ and I warned you concerning the first [of your dough]. The soul I placed within you is called a ‘lamp,’ and I warned you concerning the lamp. If you observe these commandments, well and good; but if not, I shall take your soul.’ The verse cited for the image is Proverbs 20:27: ‘The soul of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all the chambers of the belly.’” Context and connection: The Gemara’s immediate discussion concerns care in three mitzvos and the gravity of neglect. Rav Tzadok reads their deeper structure: niddah repairs ruach and blood, challah relates to the earthly nefesh, and Shabbos light addresses the neshamah. This threefold correspondence is his interpretation, not the Gemara’s explicit enumeration of soul-levels.
column13: “And the three letters of Adam correspond to the three soul divisions of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah deriving from the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah which extend from the World of the Throne downward; their physical dwellings residing in the brain (Mo'ach - Neshamah), heart (Lev - Ruach), and liver (Kaved - Nefesh), as is known.”

column15: “And God said to Moshe, ascend to Me, to the mountain and I will be there ….” (Shemot, 24:12)“To the mountain” means to the end of the renewal of all levels. column11: Genesis 2:6–7; 1:24. English translation of source: “Genesis 2:6–7: ‘A mist rose from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground. Then the Lord God formed the human being from dust of the ground, breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living soul.’ Genesis 1:24: ‘God said: Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds; and it was so.’” Context and connection: The Midrash likens the first human’s formation to the making of dough. Rav Tzadok therefore associates challah—separating sanctity from flour and water—with the repair of nefesh, the vital force within embodied life. The analogy goes beyond the literal wording of Bereishis.

column11: Sotah 5a, with Tosafos ad loc.. English translation of source: “Sotah 5a: ‘Rabbi Alexandri said: Anyone who possesses haughtiness—even a light wind stirs him, for it is written, ‘The wicked are like the troubled sea, for it cannot rest.’ And if the sea, which contains so many quarter-measures [of water], is stirred by a slight wind, then a human being, in whose body there is only a quarter-log of blood, all the more so!’ Tosafos, s.v. ‘A person who has only a quarter-log of blood’: ‘Rabbeinu Chananel explains: This is the clear blood upon which the heart is sustained; its weight is only twenty-five sela, which is a quarter of a log.’” Context and connection: This distinction serves a specific purpose in his argument. The bodily blood of the organs represents nefesh, whereas the refined vitality of the heart corresponds to ruach. Accordingly he connects the niddah-related repair to the place where inner emotional and spiritual life is situated. The precise physiological language belongs to the traditional exegetical model, not modern anatomy.

column13: “my friend, the eminent and pious Rabbi Eliezer Tzvi Ziegelman, may his lamp shine, remarked: it is named after the verse, "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" [Exodus 10:23], since the first treatise in this holy work discusses the exile and Exodus from Egypt, thus far his words. column11: Beitzah 16a; Exodus 31:17. English translation of source: “‘Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: The Holy One, blessed be He, gives a person an additional soul on the eve of Shabbos, and at the departure of Shabbos it is taken from him, as it says, ‘He ceased and was refreshed [vayinafash]’ [Exodus 31:17]. column11: Sanhedrin 91b; Genesis 4:7. column11: Zohar I, Vayeira 117a (quotation preserved in Pri Tzaddik). English translation of source: “‘When the letter vav is completed within ten six times, there are sixty [stages] to raise [it] from the dust. At each sixty of that sixth millennium, the heh gains strength and rises through its levels. In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, together with the springs of wisdom below; and the world will be prepared to enter the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, when the sun begins to set, to enter Shabbos. ... Your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the springs of the great deep broke open’ [Genesis 7:11].’” Context and connection: These are the central clauses explicitly transmitted in Rav Tzadok’s text. His explanation identifies the upper opening with the illumination of Written Torah and the lower wellsprings with Oral Torah and inner transformation; the image is interpreted within his account of teshuvah and yesod, not as a claim about any particular technology. The exact Zohar pagination varies by edition.

column11: Psalms 90:4. column11: Sanhedrin 97a. English translation of source: “‘Rav Ketina said: The world lasts six thousand years, and for one [thousand years] it is desolate, as it says, ‘And the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day’ [Isaiah 2:11]. Abaye said: For two [thousand years] it is desolate, as it says, ‘After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live before Him’ [Hosea 6:2].’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok cites the seven-thousand-year pattern and relates it to the six days of creation followed by Shabbos. His further division of the millennia according to divine attributes supplies the conceptual bridge to Noach’s six-hundredth year. The passage should be read as theological symbolism within the rabbinic discussion, not as an independently verified prediction.
column12: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot, segment 1
column13: “for one who stands in darkness encounters darkness first, followed by the light. And so was the historic order of the world: two thousand years of void (Tohu), followed by two thousand years of Torah (Sanhedrin 97a); but for one who stands in the daylight, daytime work comes first, followed by the night to rest from his labor;”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 6 (§2)
column15: Thus is it written (Yeshahya, 33:19), “of a stammering tongue, of no understanding,” meaning that it has no root of life in its heart, for understanding is in the heart. With the generation of the division of mankind (builders of the tower of Babel), even though they spoke in the holy tongue, their language was not from the root of life, but rather lip service.

column11: Isaiah 3:10; Chagigah 12a. English translation of source: “Isaiah 3:10: ‘Say of the righteous that it shall be good, for they will eat the fruit of their deeds.’ Chagigah 12a: ‘Rabbi Elazar said: By the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, created on the first day, Adam could look from one end of the world to the other. When the Holy One saw the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion, and saw that their deeds were corrupt, He arose and concealed it from them, as it says, ‘Their light is withheld from the wicked’ [Job 38:15]. For whom did He conceal it? For the righteous in the future, as it says, ‘God saw that the light was good’; and ‘good’ means the righteous, as it says, ‘Say of the righteous that it is good.’’” Context and connection: The link is pivotal for Rav Tzadok: the flood generation’s failure entails loss of access to this higher light, but the righteous person who preserves the covenant becomes a vessel for it. The discussion of the second day’s missing ‘good’ is a related midrashic theme rather than the main argument of Chagigah 12a.
column13: “Rather, it is because Hashem willed that His divine light should clothe itself within the cognitive grasp and vessel of creation; and since the primordial light was still completely overt and transcendent before creation, and creation possesses no capacity to absorb such an explicit, unmasked light, this condition is perceived from the vantage point of creation as “darkness”; as it is stated in the Holy Zohar (Balak 204b): “The primordial light with which the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world — the world was unable to endure it. What did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? He fashioned light within light, and glory within glory, to enclothe one within the other.””
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 12:9
column15: And the phenomenon that sometimes a righteous man fathers a wicked son, stems from evil lingering in his heart's depth that has not yet been refined. And that is: because all creatures were created with an innate lack; yet man on his part must ensure that at least the deficiency does not expand more than it existed upon his emergence from his mother's womb, rather conceal it lest it show outward, as written (Exodus 28:42): “And you shall make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness.”

column11: Niddah 13b; Genesis 38:9–10. English translation of source: “Niddah 13b: ‘The Sages taught: Converts and those who ‘play with children’ delay the Messiah. ... But what does ‘those who play with children’ mean? If it refers to intercourse between males, those who do so are liable to stoning! Rather, [the discussion concerns] intercourse by way of other limbs, and these are ‘people of the Flood.’’ Genesis 38:9–10: ‘Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. When he came to his brother’s wife, he wasted [his seed] upon the ground so as not to give offspring to his brother. What he did was evil in the eyes of the Lord, and He put him to death also.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok invokes the Flood generation as the paradigmatic corruption of the covenantal power of yesod. The source supplies the severity of the comparison; his further connection of the generation’s failing to the sixth day, the sixth millennium and the spiritual work of restoration is an interpretive expansion.
column13: “Now behold, it is known that the primary sin of the Generation of the Flood lay predominantly in the blemish of the Covenant (immorality), as it is stated: 'for all flesh had corrupted its way, etc.'; and Abraham knew that his seed would stem from the souls of the Generation of the Flood who stumbled in the sin of blemish of the Covenant, and the Land of Israel does not tolerate such sinners,”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 3 (§3)
column15: When God said, “let us make a man,” He was addressing the entirety of creation, summoning every part of creation to give of its power and join in the creation of man, so that man would have a portion in all of them. Then, if man should need anything, they would all be able to help him, for his evil behavior would harm them, as in the generation of the flood, while his good behavior would benefit them.

column11: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 16; Genesis 11:1. English translation of source: “‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: They instituted the joining of courtyards [eiruvei chatzeiros] only for the sake of peace. How so? A woman sends her son to her neighbor, and the neighbor bends down and kisses him. His mother says: ‘She truly loves him,’ and affection for her enters her heart; thus, through the eiruv, they make peace. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: ‘I make peace in My world, but these wicked ones are setting out to bring strife into the world.’ How do we know that they disputed with the Holy One? From the verse that begins the matter: ‘And the whole earth was of one language and of united words’ [Genesis 11:1].’” Context and connection: An eruv makes distinct homes function cooperatively; the word itself suggests joining. But the Midrash shows why uniform language and collective effort are not sufficient. Rav Tzadok contrasts unity ordered toward Hashem’s peace with an alliance organized around rebellion.
column12: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach, teaching 1
column13: “The concept of the Ark is that Hashem, blessed be He, gave counsel and protection to Noah until the days of wrath passed, and likewise for anyone whose heart has not yet been purified, he can learn strategies how to conceal himself and protect himself from every evil that rages in the world; and so our Sages of blessed memory said (Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 6): if a person sees afflictions coming upon him, let him run to the innermost chambers of Torah, and she gives him counsel how to be saved.”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
column15: “And these are the generations of Yitzchak, son of Avraham: Avraham begot Yitzchak” (Genesis 25:19). Scripture states: “Know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart; if you seek Him, He will be found by you” (I Chronicles 28:9). Abraham represents the initial awakening of chessed given from Above, whereas Isaac represents the arduous inner labor of fear and self-refinement through which a person makes that divine illumination his own permanent acquisition.

column11: Sanhedrin 71b. English translation of source: “‘The wine and sleep of the wicked are good for them and good for the world; the wine and sleep of the righteous are bad for them and bad for the world. The dispersal of the wicked is good for them and good for the world; the dispersal of the righteous is bad for them and bad for the world. The gathering of the wicked is bad for them and bad for the world; the gathering of the righteous is good for them and good for the world.’” Context and connection: The same social phenomenon—people coming together—can bring blessing or destruction, depending on the moral character and purpose of the assembly. Rav Tzadok uses the principle to explain why the apparent solidarity of the Tower generation was not the unity of holiness.
column12: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Noach, teaching 1
column13: “And behold, this was the central, quintessential utterance for the entire developmental unfolding of Creation, that they should desire unity and not be separated; for previously, when the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Noah: "The end of all flesh has come before Me, etc.", he did not plead for mercy upon his generation; however, afterward the Holy One, blessed be He, placed into the heart of all created beings that they should yearn for unity, like Abraham who beseeched mercy for Sodom, and Moses, even though the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "And I will make of you a great nation", said: "Blot me out, I pray You", because Creation now desired collective unity.”
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 12:3
column15: Whenever the Holy One scrutinizes the deeds of the wicked and overturns them, they have no remedy; He overturned the deeds of the Flood generation and they had no survival, as said: “and He blotted out all existence”.

column11: Genesis 1:31; Bereishis Rabbah 9. English translation of source: “Genesis 1:31: ‘God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning—the sixth day.’ Bereishis Rabbah 9: ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: ‘Behold, it was very good’—this refers to this world; ‘behold, it was very good’—this refers to the World to Come; the Holy One looked at both in one glance.’ Another teaching says: ‘ ‘Behold, it was very good’—this is the good inclination; ‘behold, it was very good’—this is the evil inclination. But is the evil inclination very good? If not for the evil inclination, a person would not build a house, marry, beget children, or engage in business.’” Context and connection: For Rav Tzadok, the sixth day corresponds to yesod, the power that should direct physical desire toward covenantal holiness. Its repair involves bringing even forces that have been diverted from the good back into their proper order. The identification of the sixth day with yesod is his mystical interpretation.
column13: “And the primary World of Rectification commenced from Noah, as it is written (Job 26:11): “The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at His rebuke.” And as my revered grandfather, of blessed memory, explained: this refers to the divine restraining rebuke (ge'arah) that remained impressed within each and every existence after the Flood — establishing that they should never again expand beyond their proper bounds — and this was the foundational establishment of the World of Rectification, endowing them with enduring existence for all eternity.”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 2
column15: On this it is written in the Midrash (Bereshit Rabba, Ch. 39:1), “Rabbi Yitzchak said a parable. A traveler was passing from place to place, and saw a city burning in flames. column11: Rosh Hashanah 18a; I Samuel 3:14. English translation of source: “‘Rava said: ‘By sacrifice and by meal-offering [the sin of Eli’s household] is not atoned’—but it is atoned by Torah. Abaye said: ‘By sacrifice and by meal-offering it is not atoned’—but it is atoned by Torah and acts of lovingkindness. Rabba and Abaye were descendants of the house of Eli: Rabba, who engaged in Torah, lived forty years; Abaye, who engaged in Torah and lovingkindness, lived sixty years.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok cites the passage because it distinguishes an ordinary route to atonement from a higher one that still remains open. His parallel is that some forms of spiritual damage require Torah’s transformative wisdom rather than merely the familiar modes of repentance.
column13: “Transgressions within the soul of an Israelite are not an essential acquisition, but merely incidental, and therefore they are subject to redemption, as it is stated: 'And He shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities' (Psalms 130:8).”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Shabbat 22b:1
column15: “Does God require its light? For forty years Israel walked by His light in the wilderness! Rather, it is a testimony to all inhabitants of the world that the Shekhinah rests within Israel.” The western lamp (ner ma’aravi) burned continually with the same measure of oil as the other lamps, testifying that within natural measure itself resides the miracle of the Divine Presence.

column11: Proverbs 4:20–22. English translation of source: “‘My son, give attention to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Do not let them depart from your eyes; keep them within your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok stresses the final phrase: Torah is not presented merely as a remedy for one isolated fault. By illuminating the heart and directing a person’s life, it offers the possibility of a healing that reaches through all the faculties affected by the original blemish.
column13: “Whoever is a Torah scholar gathers souls and collects holy sparks from sacred souls that have been scattered into the depths of the great abyss. Through his Torah study, every spoken word of Torah extracts those souls affiliated with him, as it is written: "and he that wins souls is wise" (Proverbs 11:30). And he also extracts his own soul, as written (Midrash Rabbah, introduction to Eichah): "the illumination within it returns him to good."”
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 44:9
column15: And from these two deficiencies are generated the skin of the foreskin (orlah) and the skin of uncovering (pri'ah): the skin of the foreskin corresponds to “my power and the might of my hand”, and this is wholly corrupt; therefore it is the commandment to excise the flesh of the foreskin and cast it away completely.

column11: Psalms 97:11. English translation of source: “‘Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for those whose hearts are upright.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok understands the righteous, particularly the person who guards the covenant and resists the yetzer, as fit to receive a higher light. He links this sown light to supernal wisdom and Written Torah; the verse supports the theme of promised illumination, while that specific Torah-mapping comes from his exposition.
column13: “The Holy One, blessed be He, His glory fills the whole earth, and there is no place devoid of Him, only that He is in deep concealment, "He made darkness His secret place" (Psalms 18:12). And when this recognition shines into man's heart—how Hashem fills the whole earth with His glory— this is termed "He brought us forth from darkness to a great light," as recited in the Haggadah.”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 15
column15: “The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord, but the prayer of the upright is His delight” (Proverbs 15:8). The upright (yesharim) are those whose hearts are free of crooked self-interest; even a simple prayer uttered from an upright, unpretentious heart brings supreme delight before the Blessed Name.

column11: Taanit 15a; Psalms 97:11. English translation of source: “‘Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: I too say that not everyone [is destined] for light, and not everyone for gladness. The righteous are [destined] for light, and the upright for gladness. The righteous for light, as it says, ‘Light is sown for the righteous’; and the upright for gladness, as it says, ‘And for the upright of heart, gladness’ [Psalm 97:11].’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok employs this rabbinic pairing to distinguish the revelation of higher light through Written Torah from the illuminating delight of Oral Torah, which straightens understanding and the heart. This identification of the two Torah dimensions is his own interpretive continuation.
column12: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot, section 2
column13: “My father, the holy Gaon of blessed memory, explained that on Shabbos there is every perfection. For from the side of the Blessed Name, there is a great expansion, as the holy Zohar states (Yisro 88a): 'By it all the supernal days are blessed.' And from the side of man there is great contraction; for whoever wishes to have a share and recognition in the spreading of His blessed light that shines on Shabbos must, for his own part, greatly contract himself.”
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 1:16
column15: Thus the Blessed Name refined the foundations, so that through spiritual labor man could attain the light and perceive that there is a divine Guide; and this is what is written (Psalms 32:2): “and in whose spirit there is no guile.”

column11: Proverbs 13:9. English translation of source: “‘The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok joins this verse to Tehillim’s ‘Light is sown for the righteous.’ Together they show both a light bestowed from above and a light that grows into joy through the right ordering of the heart. In his reading, this points to the relationship between Written and Oral Torah.
column13: “my friend, the eminent and pious Rabbi Eliezer Tzvi Ziegelman, may his lamp shine, remarked: it is named after the verse, "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" [Exodus 10:23], since the first treatise in this holy work discusses the exile and Exodus from Egypt, thus far his words. But in my view, it is named after the verse (Psalms 97:11): "Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart." And it is stated in the holy Zohar (I, 45b) and in Zohar Chadash (Bereishit 8c): When the Holy One, blessed be He, gazed upon those generations of the wicked, He concealed the primordial light for the righteous, as it is written: "Light is sown for the righteous, etc."; see there. And in Sefer HaBahir (sec. 147) on this verse: The Holy One, blessed be He, took from His good light and included within it the thirty-two paths of Wisdom, bestowing it upon this world... which is none other than the treasury of the Oral Torah; see there.”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Writings, Proverbs 16
column15: “The arrangements of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord… The Lord has made everything for His purpose, yes, even the wicked for the day of evil” (Proverbs 16:1, 4). Even the opposing forces in creation were formed solely to clarify and elevate the heart of man, so that through overcoming them he recognizes that every step is guided by the Blessed Name.

column11: Genesis 7:11. English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month—on that very day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of heaven were opened.’” Context and connection: The Zohar makes the year-number a symbolic sign for the sixth millennium: earthly wellsprings and heavenly openings correspond to different manifestations of wisdom. Rav Tzadok’s reading reverses the Flood’s destructive imagery into the possibility of a new release of Torah illumination capable of helping a person return.
column12: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach, teaching 3
column13: “Behold, this thought of Hashem, blessed be He, became known to Noah inasmuch as profound awe was ingrained in his heart after the Deluge, that it is inappropriate for man to expand himself unchecked according to his own desire, and he must only restrain his spirit; from this he understood that such was likewise the will of Hashem, blessed be He, that He would not curse the ground anymore.”
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 33:1
column15: “And Malki-Tzedek, etc., and he was a priest of God Most High, and he blessed him, and said: Blessed be Avram of God Most High... and blessed be God Most High, etc.” (Genesis 14:18–20). In the holy Zohar (Lech Lecha 87a): “The Holy One sought to bring forth the Priesthood from Shem, as it is written: 'Blessed be Avram of God Most High', once he preceded Abraham's blessing to the blessing of his Master, Abraham said to him: Does one precede the servant's blessing to his Master's blessing?!

column11: Genesis 6:9. English translation of source: “‘These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, wholehearted in his generations; Noah walked with God.’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok gives ‘righteous’ its further kabbalistic force: the tzaddik is connected with yesod, the covenantal foundation. Because Noach resisted his generation’s corruption, the six-hundredth year of his life becomes an apt symbolic marker for the point called yesod within yesod.
column12: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach, teaching 7
column13: “and it is brought in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 39:7): the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Abraham our father: You I exempt from honoring a father. The concept in this is that with Noah Hashem likewise sealed a covenant, yet the covenant sealed with Noah was not in the manner He sealed with Abraham our father, peace be upon him; for with Noah Hashem, blessed be He, sealed a covenant according to derekh eretz (natural worldly order) as explained, and as it is stated: 'And I will establish My covenant with you; neither shall all flesh be cut off anymore', since following the awe of the Deluge he accepted upon himself not to expand unchecked as mentioned, and Hashem, blessed be He, likewise agreed not to destroy the world, and Noah began to engage in derekh eretz,”
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 49:2
column15: My revered father, of blessed memory, explained: Noah expanded himself here into the three matters that were hinted in the architecture of the Ark, concerning which it was said to him (Genesis 6:16): “with lower, second, and third stories shall you make it,”

column11: Zohar, Pinchas 10:58-12:70: “In the Zohar (Pinchas, Ra’aya Meheimna III 216b), it is further expounded that in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, when the fountains of the great deep and the windows of heaven opened, the soul of Moses was ready to draw down the Written and Oral Torah as waters of blessing, but because the generation spurned God’s ways, those waters turned into the judgment of the Flood.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 6, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Pinchas 10:58-12:70) to illuminate his exposition here (“who was present then, as stated in Ra'aya Meheimna (Zohar Part III, 216b); yet the Generation of the Flood refused to receive it, and as written (Shemot Rabbah, Parashah 30) on the verse ‘And the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For every matter the Blessed Name seeks to bring into the world or unto man extends into various manifestations, containing its opposite as well, Heaven forbid, as stated (Shemot Rabbah 30; Zohar III:216b) concerning the Generation of the Flood, that they were destined to receive the Torah had they merited, and so in every generation and within every person.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:15

column11: Zohar I, Vayeira 117a (conclusion as preserved in Pri Tzaddik). English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, and the springs of wisdom below, and the world will be readied to enter into the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, once the sun has begun to set, to enter into Shabbos. So too [with the world]. And your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the fountains of the great deep burst open’ [Genesis 7:11].’” Context and connection: The sequence of images is essential: opening wisdom is preparation for a sanctified seventh period, not an end in itself. Rav Tzadok interprets the number six hundred through the six middos and the human task of refining desire; the final approach to Shabbos denotes a divine completion beyond human effort. The wording follows the excerpt in Pri Tzaddik because Zohar editions use differing foliation.
column12: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 1, paragraphs 48, 49, 50, 51
column13: “And this is what the Talmud states (Sanhedrin 97a): “Six thousand years the world will exist”; which refers to the temporal garments of this world that will dissolve in the Seventh Millennium, having boundaries in time just as they hold boundaries across the six dimensions of space, whereupon the inward essence and divine depth will radiate eternally. Therefore one illuminated by the Sabbath light, looking solely into the essence within the garments, cleaves to the light that transcends all boundaries.”
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Emor 8
column15: “And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel” (Leviticus 22:32), juxtaposed with the counting of the Omer and the festivals: through counting each day of the Omer and refining the forty-nine gates of the heart one step at a time, Israel draws down the holiness of the Blessed Name into the flow of time itself.

column11: Psalms 112:5: ‘All goes well with those who lend generously,who conduct affairs with equity.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 7, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Psalms 112:5) to illuminate his exposition here (“In the holy Zohar on this parashah (60a), Rabbi Yehudah opened with the verse, 'Good is the man who is gracious and lends' (Psalms 112:5). One interpretation says that 'good man' is the Holy One,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: This is the first tzimtzum by which the Name Havayah becomes apprehensible to another, through these powers that establish and support it. This is what the Zohar, 81a, means when it calls Netzach and Hod the garments of Kudsha Brich Hu. A garment covers and slightly dims the intense brightness of the one clothed within it, so that through the garment we are able to look upon the one who is clothed.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 18
column15: 1–5: “Make you an ark of gopher wood, etc.” The nature of this counsel corresponds to Zohar Noach (68a): Rabbi Chiyya opened: “‘Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him?’ Come and see: when a man sins before his Master and seeks to conceal himself, the Holy One executes judgment upon him publicly; but when a man purifies himself, the Holy One desires to hide him so he not be seen on the day of wrath, as written: ‘Hide yourself for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.’”

column11: Psalms 145:9: ‘GOD is good to all,and divine mercy is upon all God’s works.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 7, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Psalms 145:9) to illuminate his exposition here (“The intention is that each interpretation follows Rabbi Yehudah's opening: 'Good man' refers to the Holy One, blessed be He, Who is called good, as it is written, 'Hashem is good to all' (Psalms...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Yet on the part of the remaining indelible impression—they retain a share! Wherefore the dorshei reshimot, investigating that remaining light, declared that all possess a portion in the World to Come through that enduring impression; and from this vantage it is impossible to uproot the name of Israel from a Jew; for even if uprooted through sins, the impression remains bearing the name of Israel; which can never be eradicated; unlike the nations whose root derives from the Serpent's defilement, where holiness never dwelled!
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 4:27

column11: Zohar, Vayikra 24:160-170: ‘‘The north wind’, he said, ‘refers to the burnt offerings which were killed on the north side (zafon) of the altar, because these atone for the thoughts which are in the recesses (mazpune) of a man’s heart. The south wind refers to the peace offerings, which were killed on the south side of the altar, because they make peace between higher and lower, and between the various quarters of the world. Therefore the bringer also eats of them and has a share in them. Of all the offerings, none are so well beloved to God as the peace offerings, because they bring harmony to upper and lower.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 7, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Vayikra 24:160-170) to illuminate his exposition here (“Rather, the letter vav denotes Tiferes, while the small vav inserted in the spelling of the letter hints at Yesod, as the Zohar (III, 11a; Zohar Chadash I, 182b) speaks of the mystery of the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Now, in a human being, the legs are what support the body. Without them, the body would have no standing or position. So too, in the inner form of man — the soul — there are powers corresponding to these, which support the soul in its existence and standing. Likewise, in our apprehension of the Divine light above us, we perceive according to our own likeness.
column14: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Numbers, Balak 3
column15: “In due time it shall be said to Jacob and to Israel: What has God wrought!” (Numbers 23:23). This corresponds to Rav’s teaching in Berakhot 17a that in the World to Come the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shekhinah—meaning that they apprehend the innermost secret of how God conducts and renews creation at every moment.
